"Don't teach your students the way you were taught; teach them the way they need to learn!"

That's one of the reasons I built VIC. Besides planning lessons and drafting parent messages, it can act as a co-teacher for one group while you teach another. short.title: The Internet Is a Fire Hydrant
short.text:
The internet is a fire hydrant, fully open. The information your students need is one droplet in that explosion. 💧

In The Future Ready Challenge I broke information literacy into four skills: identify it, locate it, evaluate it, and use it.

Swipe for all four. Which one do your students struggle with most? 👇

#teachersofinstagram #teachertok #informationliteracy #digitalliteracy #librarians #futureready

linkedin.pdf_title: Teach Kids to Find the One Drop They Need
linkedin.text:
"The amount of information on the Internet is like water coming out of a fire hydrant fully open."

I used that image in The Future Ready Challenge because our students aren't short on information. They're flooded with it. The skill they need is finding the one droplet that matters.

In the book I described information literacy as our ability to control the sheer amount of information available by identifying it, locating it, evaluating it, and using it. Four steps:

1. Identify: name exactly what you need to know before you search.
2. Locate: go past the first result to strong sources.
3. Evaluate: who wrote it, when, why, and can you confirm it somewhere else?
4. Use: make something with it. Possessing the information and being able to connect the dots are two very different things.

The slides are ready to share with your staff or your library team. More free guides and classroom resources: https://www.drrobfurman.com/resources

Which of the four do your students struggle with most?

#InformationLiteracy #DigitalLiteracy #Teaching #FutureReady

short.title: The Lessons You Still Remember
short.text:
"I guarantee the lessons you remember from childhood were the ones where you participated in a unique and creative way."

Nobody remembers page 47, numbers 1 through 30. 📄

What's the one lesson from school you still remember? Tell me in the comments 👇

The idea comes from my book The Future Ready Challenge. My books and free guides are linked in my bio.

#teachersofinstagram #teachertok #projectbasedlearning #studentengagement #futureready #teachers

linkedin.text:
"I guarantee the lessons you remember from childhood were the ones where you participated in a unique and creative way."

I wrote that in The Future Ready Challenge, and I stand by the guarantee. Think back. You probably don't remember the worksheet. You remember the day you built something, acted something out, or argued for something you believed.

If that's what sticks, it should shape how we plan. Not every lesson can be a production. But every unit can have one moment students will still be talking about at dinner.

This is the work I bring into schools: keynotes and workshops on building learning that sticks, and on using AI without handing over the judgment. If your district is planning a PD day or a conference session, start here: https://www.drrobfurman.com/speaking

So here's my question for teachers and school leaders: what's the one lesson from your own school years that you still remember? And what made it stick?

days.label: What would you do? The Birthday Cookies

short.title: Principals: What Would You Do?
short.first_comment: What I did: I wrote the teacher up. The parent had every right to bring it to us, but my decision came from the facts. The teacher broke the homemade-food policy, didn't notice which child was left out, and took two cookies herself before making sure every student was included. She was the adult in the room. Her job was to make the moment safe, fair, and inclusive before enjoying the celebration herself. An adult's job is to notice before a child has to ask.
short.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

A mom calls. Her daughter was the only child in class who didn't get a birthday cookie. The cookies were homemade, which breaks the school's allergy policy. The teacher let the birthday girl hand them out to whoever she wanted. One girl got none. The teacher said they ran out, but she had eaten two herself.

A quiet talk, or a write-up? Comment your call. What I did is in the first comment.

This is one of 12 real scenarios in my What Would You Do? deck, where you make the call before you see how I handled it. That and my free leadership simulation are both linked in my bio.

linkedin.text:
Principals: what would you do?

A parent calls, upset. Her daughter was the only student in the class who didn't get a birthday cookie.

The birthday child's mother had sent homemade cookies, even though the school doesn't allow homemade food in classrooms because of allergies. The teacher handed the cookies to the birthday child and told her to pass them out to whoever she wanted. One girl got nothing. The teacher said they ran out, but she had eaten two herself without making sure every child had one.

It sounds small. To the child who was left out, it wasn't.

When a small classroom moment makes one child feel invisible, how big is the adult responsibility? A conversation, or a write-up?

What I did is in the first comment.

This is one of the 12 scenarios in my What Would You Do? deck. You make the call, then you see how I handled it, and why: https://www.drrobfurman.com/resources/what-would-you-do

short.text:

We can't fully picture the world they'll walk into. That's exactly why we need students who can take the current technology and say, "But what if?"
